book: 002 - The Simpsons and Philosophy - The D'oh! of Homer

chapters.relation: Contains the book's first five character essays. Halwani grades Homer against Aristotle's four character types (virtuous, continent, incontinent, vicious), finding outright vice in gluttony (eating Frank Grimes's marked sandwich in 'Homer's Enemy', the 64 slices of American cheese), no practical wisdom (the Bear Patrol fallacy in 'Much Apu About Nothing'), and no genuine friendship, yet argues Homer remains admirable for an unregulated 'love of life' — his 'in-your-face humanity'. Skoble uses Lisa (mocked at school, vindicated by Homer in 'Lisa the Skeptic', defeated by Malibu Stacy) to diagnose America's love-hate relationship with expertise and its slide from democratic equality into relativism. Bronson reads Maggie's silence through Sartre's study of the speechless child Flaubert in The Family Idiot and through Eastern traditions (the Tao Te Ching's 'those who know don't talk', Zen spontaneity), asking whether her wordlessness is idiocy or a species of enlightenment. Erion and Zeccardi present Marge as an Aristotelian virtue-ethicist who hits the mean between extremes and follows conscience over divine command (contra Ned Flanders, invoking Plato's Euthyphro dilemma), while Conard tests Bart against Nietzsche's self-creating Übermensch and finds him merely reactive — as 'Bart's Inner Child' shows, his rebel identity collapses when everyone imitates him — concluding Bart exemplifies the nihilistic danger of the post-Nietzschean age rather than Nietzsche's ideal.

chapters.file: ch04 - Part III I Didn’t Do It Ethics and The Simpsons.md
chapters.relation: Contains four essays on the show's aesthetics and politics. Irwin and Lombardo define allusion as intended reference beyond mere substitution (the unsuccessful shrimp company gag riffing on Forrest Gump, the Ayn Rand School for Tots in 'A Streetcar Named Marge') and argue allusions yield aesthetic pleasure, forge intimacy and community between writers and fans, and demand cultural literacy. Knight reads 'Bart the Murderer' as popular parody — comic homage rather than Hutcheon-style ironic critique — which incorporates the gangster genre (Goodfellas, The Public Enemy, the ascent-and-fall arc) into its own narrative via Fat Tony, arguing the show's version of the genre is selective and ends with Bart's return to family instead of punishment. Matheson argues The Simpsons is quotational and hyper-ironic: it puts forward positions only to undercut them ('Scenes from the Class Struggle in Springfield' feints at family values while exposing the club as warm and Marge as classist; Frank Grimes's death met with laughter), tying this to the contemporary crisis of authority in Kuhn, Feyerabend, Rorty's Derrida, and Danto's end of art, with heart-warming endings existing only to let viewers tolerate more cruelty. The Snows document Springfield's roughly 4:1 male-to-female character ratio and male-dominated episode focus, read Marge as Virginia Woolf's 'Angel in the House' inherited from 1950s sitcom wives, and argue that despite Lisa's 'Idealist in the House' role the show extends a conservative sexual politics.

holes.name: Linda Hutcheon
holes.what: Canadian literary theorist whose A Theory of Parody defines parody as self-conscious 'repetition with difference' that ironically critiques its target text.
holes.why: Deborah Knight's essay on 'Bart the Murderer' builds its entire argument by testing and rejecting Hutcheon's high-art theory of parody in favor of a notion of popular parody as homage.

holes.name: Popular Parody (homage vs. art parody)
holes.what: Parody in mass media that works primarily through comic homage to a beloved genre or text (repetition with comic rather than ironic effect), as opposed to the self-reflexive art parody of high-culture criticism.
holes.why: Knight's essay argues 'Bart the Murderer' parodies the gangster film out of fondness rather than critical irony, and no existing slug (e.g. philosophy-of-art) captures this specific distinction.
